excerpt: When war broke out in the Pacific, Army nurse Sally Millett was swept from Fort Stotsenburg to the jungles of Bataan and the gates of Santo Tomas. A reflective narrative on duty, hunger, makeshift repairs, and the quiet endurance of a three-and-a-half-year shift.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
There is a popular notion that a profession is something you put on in the morning like a clean apron and hang behind the door at night when the bell rings. But a nurse is constructed differently. Once the trade gets into the marrow of her bones, it stays there, impervious to weather, orders, or barbed wire.

In June 1941, Ethel "Sally" Blaine arrived in the Philippines, having volunteered for duty because she wanted to see the islands while they were still under the American flag. At Fort Stotsenburg, life was initially like a picnic, governed by the old regime of formal white uniforms for men and long dresses for women at six o’clock. But that orderly universe vanished on the morning of December 8, 1941, when the world changed its shape in a black cloud of smoke from Clark Field that looked remarkably like a Kansas tornado.

Formally speaking, the nurses were soon swept into the jungle of Bataan, stationed at Hospital No. 2 along the Real River. There, beds were laid directly on the bare dirt, water was hauled in buckets from a creek to bathe patients, and meals dwindled down to meager rations. By April 8, 1942, as the front collapsed, the nurses were ordered out under immense stress. After a grueling journey down dusty roads past exploding ammunition dumps and a swift boat crossing to Corregidor, Sally boarded a PBY patrol bomber on April 29, 1942, under the cover of the Emperor's birthday, hoping to fly south to freedom.

Then the boat hit a rock.

On a fresh-water lake in Mindanao, after taking on extra gasoline, the plane took on a sudden, unwelcome load of water. With the hull breached by three big holes, nurse Rosemary Hogan did what anyone with a stout heart and a tennis jacket would do: she stuffed her terry-cloth tennis jacket into the jagged hole, holding it fast with the water rising steadily to her neck until she stood submerged to the shoulders. It was a gallant effort against a sinking world, but the mathematics of the lake won out, leaving the cabin water ankle-deep as they scrambled out.

![Sally Millet](/assets/uploads/cms/sallymillet.jpg "Capt. Ethel \"Sally\" Blaine Millet")

Stranded, the group spent days running back and forth from one place to another seeking safety from the Japanese.They stayed at Lindsey airstrip for about three days, hoping an evacuation plane would make it through from Australia.While the men worked for hours repairing the damaged aircraft using Elmer's glue, army blankets, and boards, the women waited, knowing their hopes were thinning. When rescue proved impossible, they were billeted at a home they called Governor Fortig’s house, where Sally lay on the dining room floor fighting yet another bout of malaria. On May 11, 1942, they were formally captured by the Japanese.

Months later, in August 1942, after being moved from Cagayan down to Davao on a dirty, filthy little boat, they were placed on a cleaner ship bound for Manila. Sick with a high fever and unable to climb or walk easily, Sally lay on the deck where a compassionate Japanese medic secured galley ice for her head. Nearby, that same medic gently patted and kissed a crying baby seventy-five times because it reminded him of the child he hadn't seen in eight long years.

Arriving at Santo Tomas internment camp, Sally stepped off the bus and was received by Bert Holland—a former efficiency expert in civilian life who coordinated hospital assignments and greeted new arrivals. Inside the camp gates,three thousand people were locked together, and the American reflex to organize took over instantly. Multimillionaires hauled garbage, bankers washed mosquito nets in the sunlight, and men sat in student chairs on the veranda, copying down recipes from *How Green Was My Valley* just to read words that tasted like butter.

Everyone stole from the Japanese, if they could, simply to cheat the hunger. Sally recalled the legendary afternoon when a caribou liver left unattended by a Japanese water pump was snatched in broad daylight, smuggled under a borrowed doctor's coat, cooked in secret, and shared among friends.

Though her recurring bouts of malaria followed her right into captivity, she and the others endured until the tanks finally rolled through the gates on the third of February 1945, bringing freedom and bedlam in equal measure.Returning home meant returning to life antebellum; it was only coming home after the long shift—except this time, it had lasted three and a half years.
